utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Naletilic and Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik. Are you ready for your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are there any protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I have announced, face distortion and pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I think the registry is making proper arrangements. We just have to wait for a while. [The witness entered court].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: The ear phone for the witness. Good afternoon, Witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good. Would you please make the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper the usher is showing to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: [Witness answered through interpreter].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: First let me give you a few instructions. You can look towards me. Let me just given you a few instructions before you start giving your testimony. Your pseudonym in this courtroom will be NJ, and that's how we are going to call you. I shall just call you Witness. We want to hide your identity and you must make sure not to disclose your identity while giving answers. If there is a risk of you giving away your identity, then I will ask the Chamber to go into the private session. Now the usher is going to show you a piece of paper. And if you see your name on that paper, you just need to say, "Yes."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And now look at the screen in front of you. Please start giving your answers when the black cursor stops. It's very important that we are -- our words do not overlap because in that case our interpreters have a very hard time interpreting and the interpretation is both into English and French so try and speak not slowly, but at a medium speed. Now the usher is going to show you the piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: Yes, that is my name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, I'm now going to ask you without giving us, uttering your name, your first name or your family name or our address, just briefly introduce yourself to the Trial Chamber, where you were born, which schools you finished?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: I finished elementary school in Potoci. I finished secondary school in Mostar. Until the army until 1994 I worked in the ATP company and after I completed army service in 1996 I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, it seems to me the witness is giving a detailed description and could we go to the private session, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we will go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, we are now in the open session, make sure you do not reveal your identity. So what do you personally know about the beginnings, about the first conflicts with the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: The first skirmishes started in early spring of 1993, in Dreznica. The problem was the HVO flag and the Muslim flag. My superiors went there and agreed that both flags should be put up on the elementary school in Dreznica. Later on, there was a period of peace but something was in the air, there was something wrong. Military delegations met, held talks, in order to avoid a conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Okay. So how did the Tihomir Misic barracks, the so-called Northern Camp, became the property of HVO? First of all, where was the BH Army in Mostar at the time, if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: I already said that the leaders of the HVO and the BH Army met, and that they agreed that the so-called, the Southern Camp, or the southern barracks would be given to the BH Army and the Northern Camp or the northern barracks would be given to the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Let us just show Their Honours -- can you just tell them where these barracks were? I'm just going to show you a map of Mostar. That's Exhibit P11. The usher is going to show you this exhibit. And if you can, can you mark the Northern Camp by number 1 and Southern Camp by number 2?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: How do you wish me to mark that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Make a circle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: This is the Northern Camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Put number 1 there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: And this is Southern Camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Put number 2 there. Did you put number 2 on Southern Camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So this is on the eastern bank of the Neretva River? In this courtroom we refer to these banks as eastern and western banks of the Neretva River?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: Yes. This is the eastern part or the left bank. Both barracks are on the eastern part of the city, or the left bank of the Neretva River.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And you were there in that -- in the barracks all the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: Can I answer? I was in the barracks all the time. I slept there. I was there all the time, because I did not have my family house. I was expelled from my family house. This is where I had a bedroom. Where I had my office. And from there, I discharged command duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell me, in the Northern Camp or the Tihomir Misic Barracks, were there members of the BH Army, i.e. were there Muslims there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: Gentlemen, members of the HVO were also Muslims. Muslims accounted for some 35 to 40 per cent of our troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Until when were you together?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: Until 30 June, 1993. And then what happened happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Can you describe the events until the 30th of June, 1993? Do you know of anything that happened in the barracks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: Yes, counsel. Something should have happened already on the 16th of April, 1993. Arif Pasalic wanted to launch an attack on Mostar on the 16th of April, 1993, but he didn't. This I learned from my friend, Hujka, who told me that Hujka would not allow his army --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You may continue now.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: He did not allow his army to participate in that attack, and that is why this attack was deferred.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Can you tell us who Hujka is and how do you know him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: Hujka was the commander -- Hujka was the commander of Muslim troops in Mostar. I know him personally because we worked for 20 years in the same company and we were good friends. Even during the war, we cooperated. I would lend him vehicles for the transport of passengers and goods, and he would return the favours to me so we did not have any secrets between the two of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Would you please be so kind and tell us his full name, his first and last name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: I know that his family name is Hujdur but nobody used his full name. He is known all over the city under his nickname, Hujka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Does -- do any barracks in Mostar carry his name, either today or did they before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: Yes. The barracks also known as the Northern Camp today carry his -- his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you personally know anything about the events on 9 May, 1993? Where were you at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: On 9 May, 1993, I was a duty officer in the barracks. At dawn, around half past 5.00, I was woken by sporadic machine-gun shooting. I put my clothes on. I went out, and I was standing there to hear where the shooting was coming from. Later on, several shells fell from the eastern to the western side of the eastern part -- southern part of Mostar. I repeat, there were several shells from the eastern to the western part of Mostar. Later on, several minutes later, I could hear several shells from the western side, which meant that fire was returned. This stopped half an hour later, and the -- there was no attack after that. Later on, I found out that on that morning, there should have been a frontal attack by the BH Army on the western part of Mostar. The commander, General Arif Pasalic, had ordered the attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: What you're saying now, this is all you heard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: Yes. This is all that I heard from my friends and Hujka, the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Where were you personally on the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: I already said that on the 9th of May, I was a duty officer and that the sporadic fire started at dawn of that day, and Hujka, with his troops, decided to join Arif -- if Hujka had decided to join Arif Pasalic on that day, the western part of Mostar would have fallen because all the army was on the defence line facing the Serbs on that day. From Buna to Dreznica. And then there was an urgent intervention, Arif realised that he couldn't do it himself and he decided to continue negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I just wanted to establish where you were. So you were in the barracks on the eastern side, and you did not leave the barracks. What you have just told us now is what you heard from Hujka and his friends or your friends?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: I did not leave the barracks at all, because I did not have an apartment, I did not have a house, and my command duty was always such that I had to be present in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, tell us, please, whether there were any conflicts inside the barracks on that day, since you told us that 35 to 40 per cent of the troops were Bosniaks or Muslims.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: Counsel, sir, amongst the drivers who belonged to my unit, there were six Muslims. They asked me what was going on. I told them I didn't know but that I would tell them as soon as I find out, which is what I did. People found it a bit strange. They were even upset a little because they were members of the HVO and whatever I knew, they knew too, so after the 9th of May, we continued working normally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Until when?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: Until the 30th of September, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly -- actually I would like to ask you several questions because I'm not supposed to lead you or anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I apologise to counsel for the interruption, the last answer given by the witness indicates that they all worked together normally until the 30th of September, 1993, and I wanted to make sure that is the correct date, which the witness wanted to give.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik, you may make some clarification for us, asking some questions to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, counsel. I was not paying attention to the record, which says that you were together in the Northern Camp with the Muslims until the 30th of September, 1993.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: No, we were together until the 30th of June, 1993. On the 30th of September, I was already hospitalised in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you have any personal knowledge as to who were members of the BH Army in Mostar? Were they locals, people from Mostar? Or from other areas as well? And what was their relationship? Did they share the same opinions, the Mostar residents and the outsiders, if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: Had only local residents been there, there would have never been a conflict between the BH Army and the HVO. However, with the arrival of both soldiers and commanders from the eastern part of Bosnia and Herzegovina, such as Gacko and Nevesinje and a number of other areas which had been cleansed by Serbs, there was a huge influx of Muslims into the Western Herzegovina. So there were quite a few newcomers involving commanders, of whom I know very little because I rarely had opportunity to meet with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Let us deal with the 30th of June now. It is sometimes said that the BH Army liberated the Northern Camp, that is the expression that is sometimes used?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: I don't know who they could have liberated the Northern Camp from because until that day, we had been a joint army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Just to clarify, were there any conflicts from the 10th of May until the 30th of June in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: Sir, there is a village called Zalik located in the immediate vicinity of the barracks. There were daily provocations with sniper fire coming from that village. Every time when this happened, we would lodge a protest, an objection, with our command, in order so that an agreement with the BH Army could be reached so that we could avoid further casualties and further damage. Two to three of our troops were killed in such provocations. However, the response was always that this had been done by some irresponsible individuals who did not care much about our two armies being together. So fire was frequently opened from the area right across -- right across from the barracks, from the area of Zalik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: What about the period before that, the beginning of May, before the 9th of May? Was there any meeting with the HVO commanders in the Northern Camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: There was no such meeting at all. Nobody came before the 9th of May. Nobody visited the barracks or the Northern Camp before that date. Had there been such visits, I would have been in the know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Were there any women members of the troops in the Northern Camp, members of the HVO, the BH Army or simply working there in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: Yes, there were two women with the command. Their names were Ljubica and Vesna. They were there to make tea or coffee for the commanders. We had female clerks as well. However, the majority of them worked in the kitchen, the HVO kitchen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: In the Northern Camp, I presume?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: Yes, in the kitchen of the Northern Camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I should like to ask Your Honours to go into private session for a moment, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we will go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Now we are in the open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I apologise for this interruption, Witness. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: So I got this call from the operation officers who told me that the commander that ordered that all of the vehicles that are on the parking lot or inside the hangars should be removed because the BH Army was going to have a military exercise there. I didn't have many vehicles in the barracks at all, because the only communication with the barracks was via wire bridge. All other communications were down. So at 12.00, we were informed that the wire bridge was also down, which was used for supplies. It was the main supply route, both for goods and for personnel. Two of our guards, Your Honours, were slain on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I know, Witness, that this must be hard for you going back to those harsh times. If you need a break, please let us know.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: Those were harsh times indeed. But if the Court needs to know the truth, I need to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Please continue. I'm not going to interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: So after this barge was no longer -- could no longer be used, we remained cut off on the left bank of the Neretva River. We had no connection, no contact, with the right bank of the Neretva. So -- and also telephone lines were down. So there was no communication whatsoever between us and this area. So all of a sudden, shouting started from the left part of the Northern Camp. We heard someone yelling, "Ustashas, Ustashas, you better surrender, else you will all be slain." And they kept shouting, "Jihad, Jihad."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Will you please slow down, witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: I was curious. I wanted to see what kind of military exercise this was since the shooting was quite severe. I went to the door, to the exit, and started to observe the area. I did not see the attack coming from the northern part because my view was blocked by one of the buildings inside the barracks. But the shooting was so loud on that morning, and it was shooting coming from infantry weapons, I wanted to check further what was going on, so I went to a nearby park to see what our policemen on duty were doing, those who were manning the gate. The shooting was awful. One could smell powder, gunpowder in the air. After I had had a better view of the situation, I realised that Mr. Hujka was standing at the gate, and having a very heated argument with a soldier wearing a camouflage uniform and a white band on his head. This white band was partly covered with a green ribbon, and I thought that they would come to blows. Soon after that, I saw Hujka falling down on his stomach, and after that, Arif Pasalic appeared with his body guards. I had to withdraw to the building of the barracks because at that moment, I realised what was going on. This lasted for a while. There was a lot of confusion, lot of commotion, shooting was coming from all sides, and we could hear them shout and sing, "Jihad, Jihad, this whole country will be Turkish." I went to the building and found there the duty operations officer, the two signals and two ladies, Vesna and Ljubica. There was also an electrician on duty there. We were getting evermore encircled.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you but what happened with these Muslims, BH Army members who were with you at the barracks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: Your Honours, gentlemen, they immediately turned their weapons and pointed them to their colleagues from the Croatian Defence Council, and they joined those who had attacked the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Just briefly tell us what happened to you after that, you and other members of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: I don't know what was going on further away from the building where I was but I remember that they started shooting with hand-held rocket launchers in order to create panic inside the building. One such shell exploded not far from a wall in the building, and I was wounded slightly in my chest. There was a lot of smoke in the corridor and shortly after that, two hand grenades were thrown in, which exploded just in front of me, near my feet. I fell down. I fell on my face. And then BH soldiers rushed in. They had kicked the door open. They were holding their machine-guns, pointing at us. They came up to me. They took off my new sneakers, they took off my belt, my pistol, and ordered those two signals to throw down their rifles, which they did. They were looking for rifles which had -- which still had warm barrels, because they thought that some of us had been shooting. Luckily, my pistol, although it was charged, it was cold, and no bullets were missing. I also had a rifle which actually belonged to the command but which I used when I went into the field. That rifle also had a cold barrel, because it had not been fired from. And they ordered all of them to leave the communications centre with their hands -- with their arms up in the air, and they ordered two of their soldiers to drag me outside the building, because I was unable to walk, and bleeding. They threw us outside the building in the park, and we were left there to wait. However, throughout that period of time, the machine-gun was pointing at me, although I was laying down on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: How many casualties did you have, tell us briefly? What was the fate of the personnel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: Counsel, sir, I know that on that morning, our chief communications officer was killed, that I was wounded and that there were a number of people wounded near the kitchen. They were trying to pull out towards the Neretva, and they were forced to swim across the river. I think that there were even more wounded personnel amongst the HVO members but they were carried by their colleagues and they all tried to cross the river. As to what happened with my people, those who were inside the barracks, that night, I don't know. I was loaded on to a van and taken to a makeshift military hospital which had been a health centre prior to the war in Mostar. I was mistreated there. They hit me and kicked me. They spat on me. They verbally abused me, asking me why I had not joined the BH Army to fight and so on and so forth. One of them kicked me in my eyes and I could not see for days. My head was terribly swollen. After that, they put me on a stretcher and took me to the hygiene department at the had health centre. They realised that I had been severely wounded, that my knee was in a very bad shape. It was all lacerated. And they said, "Just take this Ustasha away. Let him die." I apologise for this. As I said, they put me on a stretcher and took me again into a van. They drove me around the town for a while. I couldn't tell you exactly where they took me. I was looking up in the sky. They unloaded me from this van outside a building and put me up in a basement. The building used to belong to an elementary school. They had their treasury there with an iron door. The room behind was two metres by two metres wide, and they left me there for four days. I was in a terrible condition. I was covered in blood. I had to urinate on myself. And then on the third day, they brought a military blanket to this room. They sprayed it with something which they said was a military disinfectant. They took me to another room where I stayed for 72 days. Gentlemen, Your Honours, my leg started festering on the 9th day. I cried. I moaned, I called for the guards. But all they said was that the chief of the military hospital, Dr. Milovic, had said, "Let the Ustasha die. Let him kick the bucket." The pain was terrible. I could feel the worms crawling up towards my head and it was only the 10th day that I was taken to the military hospital where they cleaned my wound. It was a surgeon from Sarajevo who treated my wound. And he placed a metal splint on my leg, and bandaged it. I was still in a lot of pain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Were there any other detainees with you? What was your fate afterwards? Were you ever exchanged?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, I think the witness seems to be having some difficulty describing these events. It's the Prosecution position that there is no dispute that the BH Army attacked the Northern Barracks on the 30th of June and captured it. That's not in dispute. Nor am I in possession of any information which gives me a basis with which to dispute or challenge the assertions now being made by the witness about his treatment after he had been captured. It seems to us that this is becoming in the nature exclusively of tu quoque evidence. I'm not certain of what other purpose that is being offered to but it's not in dispute, the Prosecutor doesn't intend to dispute that aspect of the witness's testimony. And I suggest that it may be possible to move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik, we sympathise with what the witness suffered during that war but as a matter of fact, this is not a subject matter of this trial. Would you please move on?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this witness is talking about very important circumstances that the Prosecution witnesses were referring to, and this witness is also referring to the events related by some Prosecution witnesses who came before this trial and I just wanted the witness to tell this Trial Chamber in very brief outlines what was his destiny, because this is also the truth about Mostar, which I believe the Trial Chamber should hear. This is not tu quoque. This is something that you should hear. I have here very specific witnesses, and I think that these things are very important. You have heard the instructions by the Honours, let me explain what tu quoque is. We have to be fair. Tu quoque means one crime cannot be defended by another crime. This has never been my intention as Defence Council. Let me just ask you whether you know how many -- where were you when were you exchanged, how many detainees were exchanged, what was their lot, on the eastern side, very briefly, one sentence maybe.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: In the 4th elementary school, there were 140 detainees, and I believe that it is very important what I'm going to say to the Honourable Court. I was the only wounded detainee out of 140. I was the only wounded who came to that prison. During my stay in the 4th elementary school, 42 severely injured soldiers were brought in and over 30 had been killed on the front line, and I was the only one there who was wounded. I was exchanged --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I apologise, those who were killed and who were injured, is that when they were forced to do some labour as detainees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President it's obviously the Trial Chamber's ruling which we will respect but we object again on the grounds of tu quoque.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I agree with you. Mr. Stringer -- Mr. Krsnik, would you please wind up your direct examination as soon as possible?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. Your Honours, I will address Your Honours after I finish with this witness, because I think when we talk about this area, that we have been talking about for 11 months, I believe that the Trial Chamber should know everything that happened there. I'm not talking about tu quoque defence but that the truth has to be heard from all sides. But we shall -- I shall go back to that after this witness, and I will put some objections in principle about everything that has been happening before this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Can you please tell us when you were exchanged and where were you exchanged?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: I was exchanged on the 9th of September, 1993, at 11.30. The ten of us who were most severely injured were exchanged. The Red Cross came on a -- UNPROFOR carrier, personnel carrier, they took us via Citluk towards Mostar towards the central hospital there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like now to show the videotape that is also -- that has already been prepared. It's a very brief video footage, and then we will finish with this witness. For the record, this is D1/433. -- Sorry, 343.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there is no text, just the picture, just -- let's just watch this video footage and we will hear a short commentary from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we just speed up a little, to avoid wasting too much time?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we speed up still a little more?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we slow down a little? And go on at a normal speed?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now speed up a little?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now slow down, actually go at a normal speed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now speed up a little, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now slow down. Normal speed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: For how long were you treated after this, and where were you treated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: I was taken to Zagreb, to a hospital. I arrived there on the 10th of September, 1993. I arrived at the Dubrava Hospital which is the former military hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Are you still under treatment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: I still have psychiatric treatment because I have been experiencing phantom symptoms. I have had eight surgeries in the nine months of that hospital and I never knew, I still don't know to this day, whether I'm going to be able to keep my leg. And besides the leg, my right elbow, my spine, my head, are full of shrapnel. I also suffer from diabetes. I have high blood pressure. And I have problems urinating. And I to this very day, visit a neuropsychiatrist, and I've been taking a number of different medicines. Counsel, sir, I would kindly ask you -- I would like to tell the Honourable Court that I have been trying to forget and forgive everything. I'm not here to try anybody or to hate anybody. For the good of my -- for my own good, for the good of my family, although I have been tortured, I've suffered, I don't know -- I've been through an ordeal, in who had -- if when some individuals in Mostar, who now know that I am here and who have called me on the telephone and threatened me. I have tried to forget and forgive. I'm here to tell you the truth and nothing but the truth. And whoever commits crimes like these shown in this footage, they have to come before the face of justice. They have to be tried, and they have to be convicted. This is the way I think. I know what the prison is. I know what it means to be detained. I know how much suffering can one go through in a prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: For the last question, can we please go to the private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we will go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, any direct examination, Mr. Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no questions for the witness, Your Honours, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Cross-examination, Mr. Stringer? Mr. Stringer, you ever to know that this witness suffered a lot during the war and we want to -- we only want to hear those relevant to this case. So I hope your cross-examination will concentrate on those areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I will indeed concentrate on that, Mr. President. As I said during one of my objections are, we do not disputes and do not in any way intend to challenge the testimony of the witness in respect of the treatment, the conditions that he received after he was captured.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, good afternoon, my name is Douglas Stringer. I'll be asking you some questions today on behalf of the Prosecution. Now, first of all, with the assistance of the usher, I'd like to show you a document, sir, it's been marked Exhibit P188.2. I think for this, we need to briefly go into private session, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We will go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'll start my question again, sir. Your position within the HVO 2nd Brigade, did it involve logistics and the care or the management of HVO vehicles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, I was strictly in charge of the care of motor vehicles carrying passengers and goods. I also dealt with all the technical requirements, such as fuel and parts, spare parts, and I had to issue a vehicle with a driver upon appropriate request, and that was usually the end of my assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did you assignment involve vehicles which carried military assets, such as artillery pieces, anti-aircraft machine-guns, weapons such as that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: If there were such things within the brigade at the time I was there, I don't remember any requests being made to that effect. There were mechanics who were in charge of such equipment, but I don't remember any such vehicle coming to my department for maintenance or repair.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Was artillery generally something that was within the authority of the operative zone level as opposed to the brigade level on which you were operating?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: I know that we have a special artillery unit, but I was never involved, nor did I have any insight into their weapons or equipment. I also believe that they only had mortars, 60 or 80 millimetre calibre mortars before the 30th of June. I never heard or saw any such -- any larger calibre guns at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Are you saying, sir, that artillery, as well as mortars, all fell within the responsibility of this artillery unit and did not fall within Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 12152 to 12159. your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: The artillery which belonged to the 2nd Brigade was not deployed on the defence line in our area of responsibility. We only had infantry trenches and infantry weapons and it was only those weapons that I could see in the HVO. As to the location of any other pieces, no, I did not have any knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall whether, on the 16th of April, 1993, the commander of the HVO 2nd Brigade, Mr. Vrljic, issued an order to attack BH Army positions in the region of Dreznica, Jasenjani?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: Never heard of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'd ask the usher to show the witness what's been marked P101.3. It is the third exhibit in the binder, not the second one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, this document is about three or four pages long. If you like, you can take a moment to look it over. Just to familiarise yourself with it. And then I'll ask you some questions.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: I understand. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Sir, I might suggest that you go to the end of the document, you can see the signature and the markings at the bottom of the document which might assist you in familiarising yourself with this. Does this appear to be an order over the signature of Ilija Vrljic, commander of the HVO 2nd Brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, this is the first time that I have this document in front of me. I see it for the first time, and I do not wish to comment on its contents, because I have never had access to this document. This type of orders never reached my level, but I think that I would have known about it at least from my colleagues, that something of this kind would happen. They would probably request a number of vehicles for the transport of personnel and weapons but again, I really do not wish to comment on this order because I see it for the first time and I really do not know whether it is accurate or not. It seems to me that an order of this kind should have been issued by an even more senior officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'll ask the witness be shown Exhibit P301.3 -- I'm sorry, P299.3. That's the second document in the -- witness, as you look that over, I will just tell you that this is or purports to be an order which, from the original language version, appears to have been issued on the 15th of April, 1993. It's an order issued by Mr. Miljenko Lasic, who is the commander of the Southeast Herzegovina operative zone of the HVO, for an operation called "Drezanac" whose purpose is to disarm all military persons in the Dreznica local community?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for interrupting my learned friend. I must react. This command was not signed by Miljenko Lasic. This is very visible from the Croatian original that I have that the Honourable Court has. So I would kindly ask the Prosecutor to show the things as they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, we made a ruling on this matter, whether a document is signed or not, whether it's authentic or not. We have already ruled that on the previous occasions. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, but in a cross-examination, you cannot misinterpret the facts. I have the Croatian original in front of me, and I can see clearly who signed it. You cannot say that it was signed by Brigadier Miljenko Lasic and confuse the witness when it is clearly not so. There is a signature which can be read and the Prosecutor -- all it takes for the Prosecutor to say who actually signed it rather than misinterpret the fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, at least from the transcript, I did not see that Mr. Stringer said this document was signed by Mr. Lasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But you may ask whether the witness is familiar with this document or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I don't know what word Mr. Krsnik was given in the Croatian language but I said issued. Is this a document or an order issued by Mr. Lasic. And again, I suggest that it's improper for counsel to testify as to whether a signature appearing on the bottom of a document is or is not the signature of the person whose name appears with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, you've, as we've been discussing this you've had a moment to look over the document now. I brought this document to your attention because you indicated you thought that such an order to attack Dreznica would have to have originated from a higher level. Sir, may I suggest to you that this document that you're looking at now, Exhibit P299.3, is such an order. That is an order originating from the operative zone level to prepare an operation to disarm military and civilian persons in Dreznica. Now, after having reviewed these two documents, and I'm not suggesting that you have seen them before, are you able to tell us whether this refreshes your recollection whether, in fact, there was an HVO operation involving the HVO 2nd Brigade in the area of Dreznica, Jasenjani, on the 16th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: As far as this document that I have in front of me, I can tell that the order was issued by Miljenko Lasic but signed by somebody else. That's one thing. Another thing, I already said that no such order would have ever come my way, because I had at my disposal machinery, machines, not troops, and thirdly, if something had indeed happened, I would have heard it from my friends, from the troops, and that's why I do not recall anything like this ever happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Sir, did you ever hear of HVO military operations occurring in Central Bosnia on the 16th -- beginning on the 16th of April, 1993? In the areas around Vitez municipality, Kiseljak municipality?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is beyond the examination-in-chief. Beyond the scope of my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik, as I said before, the cross-examination is allowed to go beyond the scope of direct examination, but the re-examination is not allowed to go beyond the scope of the cross-examination. This is the rules we set at the very beginning of this trial. You may proceed, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and just for the record I think this is within the scope of the direct because the witness was asked on direct about his knowledge of any conflicts that occurred between the two sides prior to May 9th, 1993, and so I -- my submission, it is within the scope of the direct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, coming back to the question, did you hear of HVO military operations occurring in the region of Vitez, Kiseljak, Busovaca municipalities, beginning, or around the 16th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, the Central Bosnia region is very specific, as regards the people residing there and I am here giving you just my personal opinion, which has nothing to do with the military aspect or strategy. I know that those people, when the Yugoslav Army attacked that region, they were exposed, they organised themselves, they put up as much resistance as they could. And the -- it was the BH Army who attacked the HVO in Central Bosnia and not the other way around. And you can learn that from a number of refugees who fled Central Bosnia and who arrived at the coast, Mostar, Croatia, and continued to travel and ended up overseas. To this very day, one-third of Croats have not returned to central Bosnia, and this is all I can tell new reply to your question, Mr. Prosecutor, and I repeat, from my own knowledge and from -- for as much as I understand politics, the army wanted to compensate for the territories that it had lost to Serbs, they wanted to compensates by taking away territories from the Croats. That's how I see things. It was not the HVO who attacked the BH Army but the other way around, the BH Army attacked the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: There was military conflict between the HVO and the Armija in Central Bosnia in mid-April, 1993. Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: I apologise. Can you repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: There was military conflict between the HVO and the Armija in Central Bosnia beginning in mid-April, 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: I do not -- I can't give you any dates. I do not have any chronological records. I had my own duty. I had my own job that I had to see that it's done properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, I think you've indicated that documents or orders such as these would not have come to you, or you would not have seen them at the time they were issued; is that correct? I'm referring now to these two orders that we have been looking at.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: There was no reason for any such document coming my way. Any document involving the troops and their movements, strategy, military analysis, I was not involved in that. All I did was looking after vehicles, oil, lubricants, fuel oil, tires, the people who drove those vehicles, and that was that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And as a result, sir, it is quite possible that this operation could have, in fact, taken place without your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: You're trying to make me say that it was so, still, if that action, operation, had taken place I would have learned it from my colleagues. I would have known about it. I do not remember that this operation took place, although the order obviously never reached me, because all of us live for successes and failures.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, in your direct testimony, you said that you had heard, I believe, that on the 9th of May, 1993, there was to have been a frontal attack by the Armija, the BH Army, against the HVO in West Mostar, but that this frontal attack was called off by Mr. Pasalic. Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: I did not say any such thing, what you have just said is not similar, even remotely similar, to what I actually said. What I said was that on 9 May, in the morning, in the dawn, there was sporadic machine-gun shooting in the southern part of Mostar, on the eastern side. This was followed by mortar shelling, again from the eastern side of Mostar towards the western side of Mostar. Some 20 minutes later, the fire was returned. I never mentioned anything about a frontal attack. I only said that the late Hujka Hujdur helped and because of his help, there was no frontal attack, and if they had launched a frontal attack, given the fact that the western part of Mostar was not a protected, they would have taken it. And that is, Mr. Prosecutor, what I said in my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: My note, sir, indicate you said also that Mr. Pasalic, on that day, had made some decision to negotiate rather than to press forward with a frontal attack. Did I misunderstand you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: I don't know what he decided, but fire stopped on both sides, and it is only logical to assume that they started negotiations with this regard because we were located in the very northern part of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So -- and you, sir, at all times, the 9th of May, and thereafter, remained at your post in the Northern Barracks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: That is correct, all the time I was in the Northern Barracks, and that is where I slept. From very rarely I would go downtown to the city, in order to sign the supply orders for fuels and oils, with our suppliers. So I had to take care of the logistics. I slept in the barracks. I dined in the barracks. That's where I stayed all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And apart from what others told you, you have no personal knowledge of what occurred in Mostar in the 9th of May, except for the shelling which you witnessed early in the morning; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: Except for the shooting in the eastern part of Mostar. I assume, and this is not documentary, I assume there were street shootings in Mostar because in the western part of Mostar, there were, at the time, about eight to 9.000 Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And again, sir, this is an assumption because you have no personal knowledge because you were not present in Mostar on the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: This is correct. I do not assert this. These are my assumptions because the shooting stopped very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, after you were captured on the 30th of June, 1993, I understand you then spent time in the custody of the BH Army, and then you were exchanged on the 9th of September, 1993, and eventually made your way to Zagreb for treatment.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: This is correct. I spent nine and a half months in treatment, all in one go.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Prior to the time you were captured, I take it that you never went to the Heliodrom, which was a military complex of the HVO located on the south side of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: I claim in full responsibility that during my -- the time that I spent in the barracks, before I was injured and captured, I was never at the Heliodrom. This is the zone of the responsibility of the 3rd Brigade and I did not have a place there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So that if any units of the Croatian Army, that is the HV, were staying or deployed in the Heliodrom, you would not have known about that? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: If there is a written trace, it could have happened. I would not have known but I would have heard from my friends that the Croatian Army came to our assistance, but I never heard that and I cannot comment upon that. The only thing I know is that volunteers from Herzegovina, who went to Croatia during the attack of the Yugoslav army on our areas, that they came back to help us, and it was ordered to them to remove the HV insignia and replace them by the HVO insignia to make us all uniform. That's as much as I know about the Croatian Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then again, sir, after you were captured, then, in the weeks and months that followed the 30th of June, 1993, you would not have been in a position to know whether HVO units were deployed anywhere in Herzegovina, because you were captured, then you were in hospital, and then you had been evacuated out to Zagreb; is that correct? I'm sorry, I meant to refer to HV, not HVO units there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, this is a very complex question. Can you please break it down to a number of questions to which I will reply one by one?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: After you were captured, after the 30th of June, 1993, you were not in a position to know whether any HV units were deployed in Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: When I was captured, and when I was detained, I fought for my life. I was barely surviving. And no military data, no strategic data, were accessible to me. The only thing I would hear, I could hear the soldiers who came to the detention, to the cell, they would say, "We will be in Split in two days. We have conquered the entire Herzegovina." And I never heard anything about the HV units. If any HV units had come to our rescue, to our assistance, I'm sure they would have beaten us even more heavily if that was true, because every failure on their part, we would feel on our skin. They would -- they would take it out on us. They never came, either to Siroki Brijeg or to Goranci, Vrde. The HVO defended its own territory on its own and it never attacked anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness in your direct examination, you were asked about Mr. Naletilic. You said, "Tell me a man who does not know Naletilic in Siroki Brijeg or in Mostar. Of course I know him but I've never met with him formally or informally. We never talked." I understand you to be saying, sir, that Mr. Naletilic was a very well known person in Mostar and Siroki Brijeg. Is that a correct interpretation of your words?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct. I said that I know Mr. Mladen Naletilic, Tuta, although we have never been introduced, either formally or informally and I would like to know a soldier in Mostar or in Siroki Brijeg who hasn't heard of Mr. Mladen Naletilic, Tuta, who deserves a lot of credit for the liberation of Mostar, because his zone of responsibility was on an entirely different part. It was far from the zone of the responsibility of the 2nd Brigade, and this is what I have to say here in front of this Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did the soldiers in Mostar and Siroki Brijeg hold Mr. Naletilic in very high regard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: I can tell you this: Mr. Naletilic came from the diaspora. He came back from the exile in 1991, 1992, I don't know exactly, and he brought a lot of his own money, in order to rally the people around the defence of their own homeland, and this is what he deserves credit for. People believed him, people held him in high regard. He helped the poor, and he helped especially those who did not have the money to even feed their own children. That is why people held Mr. Naletilic in such a high regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In your direct examination, you said of him, "We never shared any command responsibilities or duties. Nor did we share the same area of defence."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: Yes, I did say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I wonder if you would agree with me, sir, that his area of defence was connected with a unit called the Convicts Battalion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: As far as I know, the first unit that was established in Siroki Brijeg was an intervention group, and I don't know when it was named Convicts Battalion. These were chosen soldiers, and this group was made up of those people whose fathers were killed in the period between 41 and 45. Or those who had been persecuted, had to flee their area, and then came back to defend their homes and these were his soldiers -- these were the soldiers who were members of this unit. And Mr. Naletilic, Tuta, deserves credit for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: After the liberation in Mostar, which I believe occurred in June of 1993 -- 1992, did that unit remain active as a military unit in 1993, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, you are asking me to give you some very confidential strategic information. I know that in Siroki Brijeg, the so-called "Siroki Brijeg Brigade" was established, and that there was also a battalion which served to assist in the most difficult circumstances. It did not have a defence line, and its commander was not Mr. Naletilic, Tuta, but a man called Cikota.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: This is a unit that was based in Siroki Brijeg?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: When people came home to change their clothes, they were in Siroki Brijeg, and they were sent wherever there was a need for them to be. You are asking me questions beyond my knowledge, beyond the scope within which I can give you the answers with any certainty. What I'm saying now is just my impressions about the overall composition of the HVO, about its task, and I don't have to have any specific knowledge about all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge about command responsibilities or duties of Mr. Naletilic during 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NJ
utterances.text: No. I don't have any knowledge or any data about the command responsibility of Mr. Mladen Naletilic, Tuta. I only know that after Cikota was killed, this intervention unit was led by Mr. Andabak, who was its commander. This is all I can tell you and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Any re-examination? Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions from Judges? It seems to me there are none. Thank you, Witness, for coming here to give your evidence. We sympathise with you that you suffered a lot during the war. All of us will wish you a good future. When the usher pulls down the blinds, he will show you out of the room.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek? Is there any document you are going to tender?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, please, if we could have admitted we would move to tender the photograph P11 as marked will be D1/99, 199, I apologise, the video clip is D1/343. That would be it, Your Honours, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, any objections, Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe the first exhibit is the witness's markings on the Mostar map. We have no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We object to the videotape on relevancy grounds and also that it's proffered primarily as tu quoque evidence and for those reasons, we object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, as for that map of Mostar marked by the witness, it is admitted into the evidence. As for the videotape, D1/343, it's not admitted because this Trial Chamber believes that videotape is not relevant to this case. Mr. Stringer, on your part, do you have any documents to tender at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: May I have one brief moment, Mr. President, to consult with Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we are going to tender only P188.2, P299.3, and P301.3. The next three documents which appear on the list are not being tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honours, this witness testified actually on 188.2, that that was his appointment, that was an appointment that included his name. We would not have an objection to that one. 299.3, actually let me go in order. 301.3, Your Honours, this witnessing had never seen this order before. These orders never reached his level. He had never even heard of this on the ground. There is no foundation for this order. The same with 299.3. The witness testified these orders would never reach his level. He had none -- does not recall seeing anything like this happening notice area or on the ground. They are all three new documents, Your Honour, so 299.3 and 301.3 the defence does not believe there has been any adequate foundation laid for admission of those two documents and again the source of the documents, the BiH embassy for 303.3, its a new source for us we usually get BiH government or some such thing, but 188.2 we don't have an objection to. The other two we do have objections to on those grounds, Your Honour, I don't think there is foundation that has been laid. The other disturbing thing, Your Honour, whiling I'm on my feet, this is becoming more and more a pattern. The very last document 821, is some witness statement from 1997 taken from some alleged person in 1997 about an event which supposedly occurred in 1995, two years after the allegations which are contained in our indictment against Mr. Naletilic. I also note that not only is Mr. Naletilic named in this report, 821, so is his co-accused, and I don't know what Mr. Par has to say about it but I'm telling you I'm very disturbed the Prosecutor couldn't have gotten it admitted into his case in chief. Your Honours would never have let this happen. It's irrelevant it's outside the scope of the indictment it's trying to prove the facts of this indictment by proof of other wrongs or other crimes that happened previously or subsequently. Now, we deny it happened at all, but I think it's highly improper and inappropriate for the Prosecution, it happens with almost every witness we have, there is one or two document that is say bad things about my client, happened outside the indictment, they never asked the witness about it, they have they are doing it so that you'll read it and they are poisoning this whole trial by doing it and I object to it. I strongly object to it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Meek, I believe that the document P821 has been admitted into the evidence as is indicated in that list. We are not going to discuss it. And your objections is registered in this transcript. And we'll tell the Prosecutor that if those documents they are not going to use they are better not to show it to us in the future. As for the document P188.2, since there is no objections from the Defence Counsel, it is admitted into the evidence. As for the documents P299.3 and document P301.3, they are not admitted into the evidence because the lack of the source, as well as the reliability of those two documents. Yes, Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President I'd just like to briefly be heard in response to the comments that have just been made by counsel. I'll take them in reverse order. Counsel are disturbed by the fact that documents go to the Trial Chamber which ultimately are not used during the cross-examination. The practice that's been required by the Trial Chamber is that the documents, if they can be used at all during the cross-examination have to be distributed before the cross-examination begins. Now, in order to have the possibility of using any potentially useful or relevant document, it has to be included. We have no choice. I don't know what the witness is going to it stay until after he's testified. And at the moment the direct examination concludes, we don't have the time to then decide what documents we want to use or don't need any more to use during the cross-examination. So to be careful and to be prudent, we have to include everything that we think might come up. That's point one. And I don't know how we can protect our ability to cross-examine based on what we think is relevant any other way. We have to include everything that might come up. There is nothing strategic or tactical about it. We are not trying to get documents before the Trial Chamber that are somehow going to taint the case or to certainly taint the deliberations. We recognise that the Trial Chamber are professional judges and experienced legal people who are ultimately going to decide what they want to accept or not accept. That's first of all. The second point which was the first one raised by counsel, in respect of P821, the document has been admitted into evidence. I could be wrong but I have pretty specific recollection that this is among the documents tendered at the beginning of the trial through the testimony of Mr. Van Hecke and it's been admitted and I certainly don't see anything improper about providing the Trial Chamber with a document that's been admitted that might be -- become relevant during the cross-examination. So with respect to learned counsel, we cannot accept the suggestions that are being made about anything improper on the part of the Prosecution. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stringer, maybe this Trial Chamber could give a suggestion as a way out of this issue. You might divide any future evidence that most likely to be used into one bundle so that you could furnish us before the cross-examination. And for those documents which might -- which are less likely to be used at your hands, whenever you use it, you could furnish us with this document. It's just a tentative suggestion to solve this issue. We have to find a middle way between the two opposite positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's just very difficult for me to envision how we could do that. And again, I think cross-examination is something that can't be scripted, and we simply don't know until very late, until really the end of the testimony, which is even more or less likely, based on the direct evidence of the witness, but we will look for ways to accommodate both the Trial Chamber and the Defence on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your cooperation. Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the Court's indulgence I should like to raise two issues which I already mentioned earlier this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, maybe Mr. Par is on this document issue. Could we hear him first? Then we'll change the subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall be very brief, Your Honours. Concerning the procedure of presenting documents, I have a question but I also have a suggestion. I don't know whether the Chamber has to receive all of these documents at the same time as the Defence. In light of that, I suggest that in view of this rule, the Prosecutor give us all of the documents that have been prepared, as has been the practice so far, and that the Chamber be given only those documents which the Prosecutor intends to use at trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, if there is no objections from the both parties, we will try that for the next witness. Yes. We will try that. Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do not wish to waste your precious time but I have to express my concerns. The Defence is indeed concerned because of the following. The document that has already been admitted, document P821, is something that we -- concerns something that we have been mentioning ever since the beginning of the trial. Of course, I will -- I have trust in your wisdom, but what do the documents dating from 1996, 1997 or 2000 have to do with this case and this indictment? What can they prove? What if Mladen Naletilic was a general or a commander with the HVO in 1995? What does that prove? Commanders are often being replaced and shifted in 1996, 1997, I do not see any link with your case. Where are the documents relating to 1993? Where are the witnesses concerning every particular month in the year of 1993? That is the period of time that should have been the main focus of the Prosecution case. Have we heard any witness, Prosecution witness, who testified to the fact that Mladen Naletilic was in charge of the overall attack in Sovici? Have we have the opportunity of hearing such testimony here before the Chamber? No. And now are we going to fight in respect of any -- every single piece of paper when we know that Ziga -- when we know that the opposing party could have forged a seal on such documents, and we all know that in the month of July, 1993, the BH Army overcame the command of the HVO. Sarajevo and Bosnia and Herzegovina are teeming with such people and such information, after three officials of the AID have been arrested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... warned you about this. If you're making submissions make submissions not allegations of facts. This is about the fifth time you've been warned about this. You must not attempt to give evidence. Deal with the law or the facts that you're complaining about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Clark, for your intervention, but Your Honours, I have to say that if justice is to be served, then we should be concerned with the individualisation of each and every count. We cannot go on hearing such general, blanket allegations in this case. Madam Judge, it has been very difficult for me to place my witnesses and organise my witnesses in this case because we did not have an adequate case to respond to. We did not have specific witnesses or rather specific times and places of incidents that happened at the Heliodrom, for instance. The whole indictment still is, and the whole case still is, quite foggy. What do we need, documents that is fall outside the scope of the indictment? I don't see any logic here, notwithstanding the nature of the legal system that we come from. But let the Prosecutor bring us specific documents and prove the specific charges. As for the tu quoque principle, this witness has clearly not been one of them. We respond to the specific time and place namely the incident which took place on the 30th of June. And the witness MM, who testified before this Chamber, and I called this particular witness to counter her testimony. The witness told us what he has been through. But what are we going to do with the crimes in some of the cases we have allegation that is Croats were attacked by Muslims and then that the Muslim were attacked by Croats. I mean this is not a hide and seek game. Things should be alleged clearly. Let the Prosecutor state specifically what happened in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Once again, this is not a hide and seek game. In this incident, for instance, the Muslims are victims and then in another one, we will have Croats and we will go on mixing dates and years and so on and so forth. We have to have a very clear case of the Prosecution before this trial. Just take the example of the Blaskic case. In that case, allegedly, it was the HVO who attacked Bosnia-Herzegovina, and then in another case, before this Tribunal, an allegation has been made by the Prosecutor that it was the HVO that came under an attack of the BH Army forces. For me, this is a clear example of hide and seek game. And that should be rectified. This is all the I have to say, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, I'll be brief but if I don't raise my voice with the Trial Chamber, it doesn't mean that I feel any less seriously about what's been said. First of all, the document, Exhibit P821, I've been informed was admitted into evidence by the Trial Chamber. It's from the Zagreb archive, about which this Trial Chamber has heard extensive evidence from Marko Prelac, as well as having other evidence, transcript evidence, before it from the people in the Zagreb archive. I take that back. That's another category of documents. Marko Prelec appeared at least twice before the Trial Chamber. The document was tendered at that time. It's been admitted into evidence. Now, it is dated outside the time frame of the indictment, Mr. President, but it's still may be relevant and we certainly intend to use this document as well as a lot of others to make submissions to this Trial Chamber about the scope and nature of Mr. Naletilic's military authorities and competences throughout the period of time that is alleged in the indictment. And things that happened before that period of time, things that happened after that period of time, can be relevant to the period of time that's covered in the indictment. Now, it comes from the Zagreb archive. It's been admitted into evidence. If counsel -- and these constant revisions of what's been said and done in this case have got to stop. The Prosecution case is over. The indictment has been something that was the subject of preliminary motions made by these accused, many, many months ago. Counsel never, in his preliminary motions, challenged the specificity, he never raised the issues which he now claims to be raising. But in any event, the sufficiency or insufficiency of the indictment is something that counsel has had an opportunity to avail himself of many months ago, and if he failed to ask for enough specificity, it's his own problem. Those are my comments, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, let us not spend much time debating on this issue. Yes, I will give you one minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. This document, P821, we have doubts as to its origin being the Croatian archives. It is part of a case which was conducted before a court in Zagreb, and there has been not a final judgement in that case, so under the presumption of innocence, this is something that we cannot discuss. That trial was never completed. This witness was an injured party in these proceedings. As to the relevance of his testimony in 1996 or -- I don't know which year in Zagreb, his testimony is not relevant in this case. These sources are very interesting. They keep changing. We have the heading here, BH embassy, for example, but we are preparing a motion concerning this issue, which you will receive very soon. The motion concerns the embassy of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and this concludes my intervention. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, as this Trial Chamber ruled last week, that there is only two criteria for the admission of the documents. That is the relevance of the documents and another matter is the probative value of the documents. And the Judges would make decisions concerning the admission of those documents out of its own discretion. We believe that document P821 has already been admitted. And we also stress here the mere admission of a document does not necessarily mean that this document gives the accurate portrayal of the facts. The decision to authorise the admission of a document is without prejudice to the value or weight which will be accorded to that document at the final stage of the trial. The objections from the Defence counsel have been registered in this transcript, and at a later stage, we will evaluate the weight of this document, taking into consideration the objections raised by the Defence counsel. Another matter, I believe, touches upon the jurisdiction of this Tribunal. It is not the jurisdiction -- within the jurisdiction of this Tribunal to understand who started the fighting and who shot the first shot in the war. We are only going to address the personal responsibilities in violation of the International Humanitarian Law. This is the very issue we are going to deal with in this Tribunal. In other words, it's very difficult to know what truth is. It is impossible to know what the truth is. We could only act according to the documents we admitted and received from the proceedings. And we also believe that tu quoque principle should be upheld. We understand that during the wars, both sides committed terrible crimes to each other, but in this particular case, the mandate of this Trial Chamber is to address what is alleged in the indictment submitted by the Prosecution. I hope the Defence counsel could understand that. Is there any other matters that the parties want to raise? Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, thank you and I'll be brief. Your Honours, as we mentioned last week we find ourselves going into recess today and not being in session again until Monday, the Prosecution having no idea of who the witnesses will be next week. The Chamber did indicate on Friday in its ruling that the Defence would give us a list of witnesses by this coming Thursday. We have to express our concern about that, Your Honour. If we get them on Thursday, that gives us one business day before court will be in session on Monday. Frankly, as of last week, there was a point last week, and I can find it in the transcript if necessary, that the Defence were prepared to give us those names the next group of names on Thursday or Friday last week. Simply escapes us as to why they cannot give us a set of names even today or certainly tomorrow. Clearly, Your Honour, the purpose of Rule 65 ter is to allow all sides and Your Honours, the Court, to be prepared to carry on these proceedings. Getting names of witnesses willy-nilly as the case continues and the order continually changing does not assist either the Chamber or the fairness of these proceedings. So, Your Honour, we would ask that the Defence provide us the names of the witnesses for next week. We would like to receive them tomorrow, at least not later than Wednesday. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, I believe that sometime last week, you promised to furnish the list of the witnesses by last Friday. This Trial Chamber made a decision last Friday, asking you to submit a list of witnesses by Thursday. That is because this Trial Chamber was taking into consideration the three days rule of those protected witnesses in the decision we made concerning the disclosure of the names of those witnesses. Are you ready to furnish the other names of the witnesses by tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, according to your instructions, we have furnished you with a list of witnesses. This has not changed. The Prosecutor has the list of our witnesses. All except for the protected ones. We did -- we have had some changes due to the illness of some witnesses but these have been the only changes. I have come across a problem. We stopped last week and now my -- the sequence of the arrival of my witnesses has changed and that's -- we have been caused a lot of problems by OLAD or we would have been cause add lot of problems by OLAD and now we have just double-checked and it is no problem. Why are we always being warned with regard to that? Our list has always been furnished on time. We are going to furnish you with a list tomorrow. Because every time we communicate with our witnesses we have to tell them, "Either be ready or do not be ready or be ready, do not be ready." It is very difficult to work with witnesses, people have their own jobs, come from all over the world. But as you have seen, in the past, we have not failed and we hope that we will not in the future, and we are going to give you the list of our first five witnesses tomorrow or by Wednesday, and the rest, the balance, will be given to you after Wednesday, the balance to make up for the first ten witnesses. If we can move to private session, I can give you the names of the first two witnesses which have -- who have been confirmed for Monday and Tuesday. I would just -- I'm trying to be as fair as possible. Let's move to the private session. I don't know the status of these witnesses and whether that status is going to change.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Now we are now in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
